title: Niki Black on AI Adoption, Billing Pressure, and the Governance Gap in Legal
author: Niki Black

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Black accepts that AI can substitute for preliminary legal tasks while preserving human judgment and verification, and materially develops the cluster by identifying two mechanisms: redistribution of work from outside counsel to in-house teams, and compounded fabrication risk across agentic workflow steps. Her staffing claims remain predictive rather than aggregate evidence.
qs: They are doing a lot of that initial work that they would have had to hand off, and they’re handing it off in much better shape, where a lot of the initial legwork is done.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central proposition: agentic AI has contested autonomy boundaries, requires continuing lawyer verification, and can compound fabricated information across connected workflow steps. It also reinforces the cluster’s concern that governance is not ready for broader action-taking autonomy.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s cautious treatment of agentic workflows: it distinguishes autonomous multi-step action from ordinary chatbot use, stresses that the category remains contested, and highlights governance risks when lawyers may not recognise agentic capabilities. It does not materially address the synthesis’s stronger claims about tacit expertise, client context or expert-designed workflow value.
qs: Part of it comes down to how you define agentic AI in the context of legal work, which is a big debate a lot of people are having.
Without even having a full definition of agentic AI, and with the fact that it’s already being built into a lot of legal technology tools, lawyers may not realize they’re using it.

st.t: Billable hour: Faster matters need not reduce profits
st.an: Black supports the synthesis’s account that hourly billing can persist despite AI efficiency because large-firm compensation and organisational structures are deeply tied to billable hours. She also supports the view that reform pressure will come from corporate buyers and boutiques using alternative fee arrangements, while treating change as prospective rather than established.
qs: And I’ve never practiced law at a large firm, but people I know well who have, and who are partners in these firms, have explained to me that the compensation structure and everything else about how those firms function are so tied into the billable hour that it’s not a matter of changing how you bill.

People leave large firms, spin up a boutique firm in one practice area, take a bunch of clients with them, and are able to use AFAs and charge in different ways that undercut and compete with hourly billing while still providing the same level of big law service, knowledge, and expertise.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Black supports the cluster’s practical continuous-learning proposition by describing selective reliance on trusted commentary rather than indiscriminate release chasing, and by urging technology-capable legal education for changing professional roles. Her contribution is qualitative and does not establish which learning or filtering practices are most effective.
qs: But for me, it’s following the blogs of people I trust and seeing what they’re saying.
They’re going to have to prepare students more for solo practice, prepare them for other types of roles, and make sure they understand how to use tech to allow them to excel in those roles.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Black supports the cluster’s account that AI is shifting preliminary work in-house, increasing pricing pressure and potentially reducing leveraged staffing. Her claims about broader staffing cuts and stronger small-firm competition are predictive and largely qualitative, while Lambert’s observations about weak current client pressure reinforce the cluster’s caution that market-wide effects remain unsettled. The source does not materially address the apprenticeship problem.
qs: They are doing a lot of that initial work that they would have had to hand off, and they’re handing it off in much better shape, where a lot of the initial legwork is done.
They’re reducing associate levels and admins, but eventually they may start cutting not only entry-level associates, but actual associates and possibly partners.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Black supports the cluster’s core view that AI is reshaping legal staffing and creating development and governance challenges rather than simply replacing lawyers. She points to reductions in associate roles, uncertainty over legal education, a need for firm-wide AI training, and continued human verification, though she does not directly develop the cluster’s proposals for funding apprenticeship or partner succession.
qs: They’re reducing associate levels and admins, but eventually they may start cutting not only entry-level associates, but actual associates and possibly partners.
I mean, I think every firm needs guidance and training on AI.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source aligns with the synthesis’s balanced view: AI may narrow the justice gap, but unequal access to reliable tools could create a two-tier system. It treats that risk as possible rather than inevitable and reinforces that technology is not a standalone solution, with greater funding also required.
qs: So there’s a real fear, I think, that AI could create a two-tiered system, premium, highly accurate AI for wealthy clients, and hallucination-prone solutions for pro se litigants.
Access to justice is not a single-shot solution.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source accepts that AI may help narrow the justice gap but explicitly rejects treating it as a sufficient solution. It reinforces the cluster’s view that meaningful access depends on complementary institutional choices, especially greater funding, while recognizing unequal-access risks as possible rather than established.
qs: Access to justice is not a single-shot solution.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: Black supports the cluster’s core proposition that legal AI’s benefits depend on adaptation rather than technology alone. She applies this particularly to legal education, urging preparation for technology-enabled roles and forecasting rapid structural change, while offering recommendations and predictions rather than measured evidence.
qs: They’re going to have to prepare students more for solo practice, prepare them for other types of roles, and make sure they understand how to use tech to allow them to excel in those roles.
So that’s going to be the biggest challenge, figuring out how to adapt within those huge changes taking place.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core account that AI’s practical effects depend on how legal work is reorganised and governed. It reinforces lawyer verification, AI-enabled insourcing, buyer-driven efficiency pressure, and possible changes to staffing and provider competition, while appropriately treating many labour and pricing effects as predictions and noting limited client visibility.
qs: And then from there, you do what you’re supposed to do, which is edit, revise, ensure accuracy, do a little legal research, and then roll it out, right?
They are doing a lot of that initial work that they would have had to hand off, and they’re handing it off in much better shape, where a lot of the initial legwork is done.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s access-to-justice strand by reporting AI-assisted self-representation and greater accessibility of complex issues, while adding that individual consumers may initially lack the sophistication to assess AI-assisted legal services. Its claims are anecdotal or predictive rather than evidence of reliable delivery, quality, or outcomes, so it does not materially extend the cluster’s implementation framework.
qs: Like it or not, AI is getting better, and it’s making some of these complicated issues more accessible for pro se litigants to bring into court.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Black supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI is restructuring legal-service production and pricing rather than eliminating lawyers. She highlights structural dependence on billable hours, buyer pressure for efficiency, technology-enabled competition, and in-house completion of preliminary work while outside counsel retains finalisation and judgment roles. Her workforce-displacement claims are more speculative than the cluster’s cautious employment assessment, but this does not alter her overall alignment.

Her claims about billing, staffing and access-to-justice effects are more predictive or anecdotal than the cluster’s broader evidence base, but they align with its cautious, selective-deployment framing.

kp.k: Individual AI adoption outpaces formal firm governance
kp.d: Discussing the 8am Legal Industry Report 2026, host Marlene Gebauer reports that 69% of legal professionals personally use general-purpose AI for work, more than double last year; 43% report no formal firm AI policy and no plans for one, and only 9% actively enforce a written policy. Black confirms the adoption jump and governance shortfall, qualifying that respondents predominantly represent solo, small and some mid-sized firms, with some large firms included. She attributes part of the gap to smaller organisations' limited governance resources and the speed of adoption. The transcript supplies no sample size.
qs: Your report notes that 69% of legal professionals are now personally using general-purpose AI tools for work, more than double from last year, I think.
Forty-three percent of respondents say that their firm has no formal AI policy and no plans to create one, and only 9% are actively enforcing a written policy.
the larger an organization gets, the more likely they are to have people devoted to governance and training. And the smaller it gets, the more of a lift that becomes.

kp.k: Small firms need guidance, training and verified AI-assisted policies
kp.d: Black recommends AI guidance and training for every firm, including self-training for solos and explicit guardrails once employees are involved. She suggests using AI to collect information and draft guidance, but requires editing, accuracy checking and legal research before implementation.
qs: I mean, I think every firm needs guidance and training on AI. And if it’s a solo, then you’re guiding and training yourself. But once you have employees, you need to have something.
And then from there, you do what you’re supposed to do, which is edit, revise, ensure accuracy, do a little legal research, and then roll it out, right?

kp.k: Sophisticated buyers may lead efficiency and pricing pressure
kp.d: Host Greg Lambert characterises client-driven pressure in the report as small and cites ACC and Everlaw data suggesting approximately 60% of corporate clients do not know whether their firms use AI. Black argues corporate counsel and insurers are better positioned than individual consumers to demand efficiency and lower costs because they understand legal work and purchasing. She expects individual-client pressure to develop more slowly, potentially increasing as those clients use AI themselves; this is her interpretation and forecast, not a measured adoption timetable.
qs: the ACC and Everlaw data indicate that something like 60% of corporate clients have no idea whether their firms are using AI or not.

So I’ve always thought you would see those two groups initially putting the pressure on to use these tools, increase efficiency, and reduce costs in a sophisticated way because they’re sophisticated consumers.
But once they start using it more and more in their own work, they may start to want to understand how lawyers are using it.

kp.k: Client AI research can help or compound legal confusion
kp.d: Lambert reports seeing increasingly sophisticated AI-assisted pro se filings. Black explicitly says she has not discussed clients' preparatory AI research with attorneys and treats it as a supposition: AI may help informed consumers but may also send others down incorrect procedural or substantive paths, creating corrective work for lawyers. She recounts an unnamed hallucination case involving numerous pro se filings and suggests AI-assisted volume can burden opposing counsel even when filings make little sense.
qs: Well, that isn’t an issue I’ve spoken to attorneys about, but I think it’s a good supposition.

So I do think, depending on the sophistication of the legal consumer, it may be helpful, or it may take longer to walk them off that path and explain to them that’s not the actual issue you’re dealing with here, and this is what you’re dealing with.
all of a sudden you’re overwhelmed with papers, some of which don’t make a lot of sense, and you have to unwind it and then respond to it.

kp.k: Client AI use raises unresolved confidentiality protection questions
kp.d: In response to Gebauer's question about client research and privilege, Black reports divergent federal district court treatments of AI-related information, describing third-party disclosure versus work-product protection. She qualifies her knowledge and acknowledges different factual scenarios. No cases are named; her account should be understood as a report of emerging, fact-dependent disagreement rather than a settled rule.
qs: There are only two courts that have even looked at that, apparently, as far as I know. And there is a split in the federal district courts about it.
It’s a little more complex, and the factual scenario is different. But essentially, one says it’s disclosed to a third party, and another says it’s work product and protected.

kp.k: Billing expectations collide with hourly compensation structures
kp.d: Gebauer reports that nearly 50% of legal professionals expect AI to change billing, with 25% expecting fewer billable hours per matter and 22% anticipating more flat fees. These are respondent expectations, not observed pricing changes. Black argues large firms will struggle to move away from hourly billing in the short term because compensation and organisational structures depend on it, citing explanations from acquaintances who practised at or are partners in such firms rather than her own large-firm experience.
qs: The report highlights that nearly 50% of legal professionals expect AI to change billing practices, with 25% expecting reduced billable hours per matter and 22% anticipating more flat fees.
the compensation structure and everything else about how those firms function are so tied into the billable hour that it’s not a matter of changing how you bill.
You’re going to have to change so many other aspects of how that firm is structured, and all the cascading things that are impacted by that.

kp.k: AI-enabled boutiques could force large-firm pricing changes
kp.d: Black predicts pressure from in-house buyers, spin-off boutiques and technologically enabled solo and small firms will push large firms toward alternative pricing. She describes boutiques retaining large-firm expertise while undercutting hourly pricing through AFAs. She also asserts firms are reducing associate and administrative staffing because of AI, without supplying supporting figures, and speculates that cuts could eventually extend beyond entry-level associates to partners.
qs: First, from in-house counsel requiring them to change it because otherwise they’re going to use someone else.
are able to use AFAs and charge in different ways that undercut and compete with hourly billing while still providing the same level of big law service, knowledge, and expertise.
They’re reducing associate levels and admins, but eventually they may start cutting not only entry-level associates, but actual associates and possibly partners. Who knows what they’re going to do.
They’re not going to do it willingly, but it’s going to happen.

kp.k: In-house AI use shifts preliminary work from outside counsel
kp.d: Black asserts that in-house teams already perform more initial work with AI and send more developed material to outside counsel for finalisation or final advice. She predicts a recently released Claude legal tool will accelerate this process, while explicitly expressing uncertainty about its exact name. No quantitative evidence of increased insourcing is supplied.
qs: They are doing a lot of that initial work that they would have had to hand off, and they’re handing it off in much better shape, where a lot of the initial legwork is done.
And then they want outside counsel to finalize the product or provide the final answer.
And the Claude for Legal tool, I’m not sure of the exact name, but that was just released, and I think it’s going to expedite that process even more.

kp.k: Embedded agents retain lawyers' output verification obligations
kp.d: Lambert cites survey usage of approximately 58% for legal research and 49% for document drafting before asking about autonomous systems. Black describes disagreement over whether closed-system retrieval and integration workflows count as agentic, considers that they do, and suggests lawyers may already use them unknowingly through legal software. She sees closed systems as somewhat less risky but insists that human review and accuracy checking remain necessary.
qs: in the survey, it showed something like 58% usage for legal research and 49% for drafting documents.
Without even having a full definition of agentic AI, and with the fact that it’s already being built into a lot of legal technology tools, lawyers may not realize they’re using it.
It’s just more of a closed system, so it reduces the risk a little. And they still have that obligation to review the output and make sure it’s accurate.

kp.k: Autonomous workflows risk cascading errors and costly verification
kp.d: Black agrees with Lambert that governance is ill-prepared for more autonomous workflows involving browsing and client files. Responding to an unnamed lawyer's LinkedIn account, she worries that fabricated information can propagate through subsequent tasks and questions whether overnight communications to opposing counsel received adequate review. Her suggestion that verification could take at least an hour is an estimate for that anecdote, not a measured productivity finding; her broader reliability criticism is likewise an expressed judgement rather than a benchmark result.
qs: And then when they take whatever they made up and apply it to something else, which is what would happen in this scenario, it becomes a game of AI telephone.
To properly review and ensure that wasn’t happening, it would take an hour, I would think, at least, to go over what it did.
I think we’re in a weird place because the tech is advancing so quickly and there is a lot of potential, but the reality still seems a little questionable when you get into things that complex.

kp.k: Justice-gap optimism depends on funding and lawyer-supported technology
kp.d: Gebauer reports that 76% of respondents are optimistic AI will narrow the access-to-justice gap, 72% identify legal-service cost as a primary barrier, and 62% of lawyers believe the rule of law is under threat. Black rejects a technology-only solution, advocating greater funding alongside guarded legal AI for legal aid lawyers, public defenders and other frontline providers. She offers one legal aid lawyer's account of increased client capacity using ChatGPT as anecdotal support and warns that without funding technology could produce a two-tiered system.
qs: A strong majority of respondents, 76%, are optimistic that AI is going to help narrow the access to justice gap. And 72% admit the sheer cost of legal services is still a primary barrier. Then 62% of lawyers agree that the rule of law itself is currently under threat.
Access to justice is not a single-shot solution. There’s no one way to solve it. You absolutely need greater funding.

I had a legal aid lawyer reach out to me after one of the articles I wrote saying that he started using ChatGPT when it first came out and was able to take on more clients because it increased his efficiency so much.
But without the funding, I think it ends up creating a two-tiered system.

kp.k: Rapid structural change requires rethinking professional preparation
kp.d: Asked about the next three to five years, Black predicts interconnected changes in pricing, competition between smaller and larger firms, and client expectations, driven substantially but not exclusively by AI. Drawing on a recent conversation with law-school deans, she argues law schools must reconsider technology teaching and prepare students for solo practice and other roles. The central challenge she identifies is adapting institutional structures quickly enough, rather than merely adopting tools.
qs: It’s all the structural impacts that are going to come from all the changes happening right now, in large part driven by AI, but not only AI.
They’re going to have to prepare students more for solo practice, prepare them for other types of roles, and make sure they understand how to use tech to allow them to excel in those roles.
And I think client expectations are going to change. It’s this major structural change that’s going to happen really quickly.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Niki Black describes rapid bottom-up adoption, lagging governance, growing competitive and pricing pressure, and significant but conditional benefits from AI.
pts.d: Black says individual generative-AI use more than doubled relative to the previous survey year, while training and policy development lag. She attributes the governance gap partly to smaller firms' limited resources and partly to adoption speed, and recommends using AI to help draft guidance subject to human checking. She expects corporate counsel and insurers to lead demands for efficiency and lower costs, with individual consumers following more slowly. She predicts that large firms will resist moving away from hourly billing because their compensation and organisational structures depend on it, but will face pressure from in-house buyers, boutique spin-offs and technology-enabled smaller firms offering comparable expertise at lower prices. She describes associate and administrative reductions as already happening because of AI and speculates that cuts could extend to more experienced associates and partners. She says in-house lawyers already use AI for preliminary work, leaving outside counsel to finalise it. She suggests client AI research can either help or create misconceptions, and AI-enabled pro se filings can increase opponents' response burden. Black regards some closed-system legal tools as already agentic, but doubts the current reliability of more autonomous, complex document workflows because fabricated information can propagate between steps. She argues that AI combined with greater funding could expand legal-aid capacity and improve representation, whereas technology without funding risks a two-tiered system. She predicts rapid structural changes in pricing, competition, client expectations and legal education.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Black draws on her organisation's survey, professional conversations, an unnamed court case, personal tool use and individual anecdotes; many market and reliability claims remain qualitative predictions or judgments.
pts.d: For adoption and governance, Black relies on the 8am Legal Industry Report 2026, which she authored, describing this as the third year of tracking generative AI. She qualifies the sample as predominantly solo, small and some mid-sized firms, with some large firms; the transcript does not supply sample size or survey methodology. Her account of large-firm billing rigidity rests on explanations from partners she knows, not her own large-firm practice experience. She refers generally to corporate-counsel data without presenting its methods or results herself. She explicitly says she has not discussed AI-prepared clients with attorneys and labels that proposition a supposition. Her litigation-burden discussion draws on one unnamed hallucination case. Her account of privilege and work-product uncertainty refers to a small number of unnamed federal district court decisions with differing facts, not a settled rule. Her concerns about autonomous workflows draw on personal experimentation and an unnamed LinkedIn post; her estimate of at least an hour to verify its purported output is a judgment, not a measured result. Her access-to-justice argument includes a legal-aid lawyer's report that ChatGPT enabled him to take more clients. Her educational forecast is informed by a recent conversation with law-school deans. No benchmarks, measured hallucination rates or quantified causal evidence for staffing reductions are presented.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Black distinguishes current adoption and workflow changes from short-term billing resistance and a broader three-to-five-year structural outlook; benefits depend on verification, buyer sophistication and funding.
pts.d: The survey discussion concerns 2026 and change from the preceding year. Black describes preliminary in-house work and some embedded agentic functionality as already present. She expects large-firm billing change to be difficult in the short term; wider competition and possible senior staffing cuts have no precise deadline. Individual clients' demands for AI transparency and efficiency may grow as they use AI in their own work. Whether client research helps depends on their legal sophistication. AI-assisted policy drafting requires editing, accuracy checks and legal research. Black says closed-system agentic tools reduce risk somewhat but do not remove lawyers' duty to verify output; her doubts about complex autonomous workflows expressly concern the current state of the technology. Her access-to-justice forecast requires better funding and dependable, guardrailed tools supporting practitioners, rather than technology alone. Her final structural forecast responds to a question about the next three to five years, while stressing rapid change and acknowledging that AI is not its only driver.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The changes affect firms of different sizes, sophisticated and individual buyers, legal workers, self-represented litigants, publicly funded practitioners and law schools in different ways.
pts.d: Solo and small firms face comparatively heavy governance burdens but may gain competitive capacity against large firms. Large firms face pressure to restructure billing and compensation, while associates, administrative staff and potentially partners face reductions. Boutique spin-offs may use alternative fee arrangements to compete with large-firm expertise. Corporate legal departments and insurers are positioned to demand efficiency and cost reductions; in-house lawyers may retain more initial work and reduce the scope handed to outside counsel. Individual clients in criminal law, family law and trusts and estates are less equipped to assess efficiency, and their AI research may require correction. Self-represented litigants can generate more submissions, increasing defence counsel's workload. Lawyers using autonomous tools retain verification responsibilities. Legal-aid lawyers, public defenders and people unable to afford counsel may benefit from increased capacity if funding and suitable tools are available. Law schools must prepare students for technology-enabled solo practice and other roles. Black contrasts this public-facing access agenda with a top-level market in which the Big Four increasingly provide legal services; enterprise competition is not itself her proposed solution to unmet legal need.
